13: What to know before you start
14: THE MOST COMMON MIX-UP IS IN THE SECOND SHEET. A bakery that sells directly to consumers is a retail food establishment and does NOT register with FDA: retail food establishments are exempt (21 CFR 1.226(c)). What it needs is a food permit from the local health department or, in New York and Florida, from the state agriculture department if it bakes and sells to go. Don't hold your opening waiting for an FDA registration nobody asked you for.
15: THE FOOD PERMIT COMES AFTER THE PRE-OPENING INSPECTION, and that cuts both ways: you can't open until it's issued, and having your plans approved doesn't mean you have it.
16: WHAT CHANGES BY STATE IS FLAGGED. The checklist has a column that says so step by step. The workbook uses four states as EXAMPLES (California, Texas, New York and Florida) because they permit the same bakery in very different ways. If yours isn't one of them, search "[your county] environmental health food facility plan check" (or "[your city] food establishment plan review"), and check your state department of agriculture too.
17: COSTS WE DON'T KNOW AREN'T MADE UP. Steps whose cost depends on your city, county or vendor say "Get a quote" in the green cell, and the summary tells you how many are still pending. A guessed number for a city fee is worse than a blank: at least you can see a blank.
18: DATES EXPIRE. Minimum wages change (check FloridaCommerce for Florida's current rate), California adjusts its cottage food sales caps every year, and Texas changed its cottage food rules on September 1, 2025. That's why all of it lives in cells and notes, not buried in a paragraph, so you can update them one at a time.
19: THIS WORKBOOK IS NOT LEGAL ADVICE. Each legal fact has a cell comment with the source (agency, rule and section) and a link, checked in October 2026. Read them and confirm them with your city, county and state; don't rely on a checkbox.
